analysis.one_liner: Creates federal-state partnerships to cover college costs so students can attend in-state public colleges without debt.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in June 2023 with 8 Senate Democrats behind it, it got no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have offered every state a federal grant equal to what it already spends on public higher education. In exchange, states would cap tuition and fees and cover the gap between what students can afford and the full cost of attendance, so students at in-state public colleges could graduate without loans. It also would fund the same promise at historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions, and make DACA recipients eligible for federal student aid.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at public colleges, especially low-income and middle-income students who currently borrow to cover costs, would see their unmet need paid by federal-state grants. HBCUs, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions would receive dedicated funding to do the same for their students. DACA recipients brought to the US as children would gain access to federal financial aid for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students at public and minority-serving colleges

how_it_helps.text: States receive a federal grant equal to their own net operating support for public higher education, roughly doubling state investment, and must use it to cover students' unmet financial need, starting with Pell Grant recipients [S3].

Participating states must cap tuition and fees at public colleges at levels on the date of enactment, allowing only inflation-based increases, and commit to reducing tuition as state investment grows [S3].
HBCUs, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions would get grants to cover their students' unmet need, with 95% of funds going directly to need-based aid [S3].
DACA recipients who entered the US before age 16 and meet education or military-service criteria would become eligible for federal student aid [S2].

Four percent of each state's grant must fund student success programs — advisors, tutors, child care, transportation, emergency aid — aimed at helping low-income students actually finish their degrees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program, authorized at $84 billion for fiscal year 2024 plus 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033. Participating states would be required to maintain their existing higher education funding and keep it at least at a three-year average level as a condition of receiving grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and participating state budgets

drawbacks.text: The price is very large: $84 billion in the first year alone, with open-ended authorizations through 2033, making this one of the biggest new federal programs in higher education [S3].

The federal grant formula matches whatever a state already spends, so states that have invested heavily in public colleges get far more federal money than low-investment states, which could reward past spending decisions rather than current need [S3].

States that join must lock in funding levels and tuition caps for years; if a state later wants to redirect money or a recession forces cuts, breaching the partnership triggers withholding or loss of the grant, limiting state budget flexibility [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students buried in loan debt, the benefit is direct and large: free tuition and covered living costs at in-state public colleges, plus help staying enrolled and graduating. The honest cost is the scale — roughly $84 billion a year and more after that — and the fact that the matching formula ties federal money to how much a state already spends, which directs more money to states with big public university systems. The bill's tuition caps and oversight provisions are real but depend entirely on future appropriations, which Congress never acted on.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the Debt-Free College Act of 2023 on June 7, 2023, joined by six other Senate Democrats: Durbin, Padilla, Welch, Merkley, Baldwin, and Booker [S3].
Seven additional Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, for a total of eight of the chamber's 48 Senate Democrats [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no further activity — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].
No House companion action appears in the record; the bill existed only as a Senate proposal [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. Lenders, for-profit colleges, and high-tuition institutions keep their market unchanged, and students continue borrowing to cover college costs. The bill's backers lost nothing but the opportunity; no one had to defend the program in a vote or hearing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; students kept borrowing

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: Lead sponsor, US Senator from Hawaii
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored the state-federal partnership design.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The HELP Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored or supported the bill, leaving it without a path to the floor in a chamber where most bills need bipartisan agreement to advance.

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters — Schatz, his six original co-introducers, and seven additional cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican ever signed on [S4].

industries.note: Would receive roughly double the state operating support through federal matching grants, with 4% earmarked for student support services, in exchange for tuition caps. State budgets for higher education would be locked in at current levels.

If students' unmet need at public colleges were covered by grants, far fewer students would need federal and private loans to attend. Lenders' interest in the bill ran opposite to debt-burdened students' interest.

The grant money is restricted to public institutions and private nonprofit minority-serving institutions; for-profit colleges get nothing, and institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit within 25 years are excluded. These schools compete with public colleges for the same students.

industries.industry: HBCUs, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: Would get a dedicated $3 billion-per-year grant program to cover their students' unmet need, conditioned on capping tuition and maintaining low-income enrollment.
